Australian Sports Guidelines
An organisation called Sports Medicine Australia has issued new
guidelines in order to improve safety for children and young adults
when playing sport. The guidelines aim to reduce preventable injury
A
Annually about one million Australians injure themselves playing sport, with the
rates of those requiring hospitalisation highest in the 6 — 14 year age group.
Altogether sports-related injuries cost an estimated $1,66 billion a year, and at
least half of them are avoidable, says Sports Medicine Australia programme
manager Amy Smithson. ‘We want children to be able to gain access to the Jong-
term health benefits of participating in sport,’ Smithson says. ‘Stopping injuries
from happening is one of the best ways to do that, and would reduce the health care
budget,’
Experts agree that the advantages of participating in sport far exceed the risks.
Physical activity helps ward off a host of medical problems including obesity, heart
disease, diabetes and osteoporosis, Beyond that, sports help children improve their
gross motor functions such as jumping and kicking, and provide an opportunity for
them to learn skills important in adult life, such ae being part of a team and getting
on with others.
Research shows that 20 per cent of adults don't participate in physical activity due
to injury they’ve incurred in the past. A random telephone survey of more than
1,000 people living in Victoria, Australia found that only a fraction of those who
participate in sport or active recreation had been injured doing that activity — 84
people out of 648, or 5 per cent. But the impact for more than 50 per cent of those
who were injured was significant: in many cases performance in the activity, ability
to participate at all, and even daily living were affected.
Meanwhile, a number of studies overseas have shown that injury is the first or
second most common reason that children drop out of sports, says Professor
Catherine Frost, an expert in sports injury prevention at the University of Ballarat,
Victoria, Australia and a co-author of the new guidelines. However, the belief about
safety and risks often doesn't reflect the reality. Research we did in New South
Wales found that more than a quarter of parents of 5- to 12-year-olds prevent their
child from participating in some sport because they are worried about safety,’ Frost
said. This occurs more commonly with boys, with 37 per cent acknowledging they'd
stopped their son from playing a particular sport for this reason. This is much
higher than it should have been, given the relatively low rate of sports injuries in
children. Mums and dads think sport is more dangerous than it really is, Frost
said. Publicity of injuries of professional sport stars, particularly Australian football
and rugby players, could be fuelling this wrong perception, she says. Reports for one
year show that Australian football was the sport most associated with
hospitalisation, which has prompted plenty of media discussion over just how safe
the game is.
Turn over >

But the sport being played by the professionals on TV and the sport children are
playing are two very different things. Injury rates in children are much, much
lower than those in elite players, and when injuries do occur, they are much less
severe,’ Frost says. The speed and intensity of alite games, and the fact that players
are pushing their bodies to their physical limite, also mean that their injuries tend
to be higher impact. ‘For all sports there is an extremely emall risk in modified
versions of the games that are usually played until around the under-12 level,’ Frost
says. A study of a junior cricket league in New South Wales found no injuries at all
in the under-8s, for example, ‘because they played such a heavily modified version
of the game,’ she says. ‘The risk increases as the form of the sport becomes more
adult.’ As you might expect, the risk of injuries goes up where there is more body
contact — but heavy tackling or contesting of the ball is often discouraged for
children.
The most common injuries in the older children were bruises and sore fingers from
being hit while batting, or not being able to catch properly while fielding. ‘Children
often get injured when they don’t have enough game skills, so learning the rules
and technique of the game properly is essential,’ Frost says. Since training in
schools has been introduced in a graduated fashion, appropriate for age and
physical ability, injury levels have dropped. Interestingly, the same logic seems to
hold true in adults as well. A study of 1500 adults who participated in weekend
sports found that those who had received training from a professional trainer were
significantly less likely to be injured, she says.
Compared with the previous guidelines, the updated version has more focus on the
responsibilities of spectators on the sidelines. The suggestions in the revised
guidelines also tend to be practical and aimed at making sports a more positive
experience for children involved. For example, they suggest ‘a games-based
approach to running that more closely resembles the stop-start behaviour of
children and young people’s play,’ as opposed to simply running laps around the
field. ‘Well planned and varied game-based activities should make up the majority
of training sessions for young participants,’ the guidelines state.
